correctness.rationale: Definitions and edge cases fully fixed: 256 four-nucleotide words, three overlap lengths, self-overlap and all pairs, reverse complementation. Exhaustive orbit graph reduces all admissible closed codes bijectively to weighted cliques; 180 unbordered words -> 56 internally feasible RC orbits (12 singleton,44 pairs), with 540 edges. Inductively valid include/exclude recurrence exhausts all cliques, evaluating 398 subset states and returning optimum 17 with 32 maximal cliques. Explicit 17-word witness is directly checked. Independent weighted coloring branch-and-bound returns the same (17,32) in 293 calls. All 32 codebooks verified for overlap and complement closure; four size-eight symmetry classes verified. Standalone verify.py is replayable; finite exhaustive proof, no extrapolation.

originality.rationale: Full-text comparisons separate general cross-bifix-free bounds (Chee 2012, Blackburn 2013) and the exact unrestricted quaternary length-four optimum 27 (Stanovnik et al. 2024, Theorem 19) from the new reverse-complement-closed optimum 17, the exact count 32 and the four orbit classes. Published research-record searches for exact parameters and synonyms returned nearby but non-covering problems. The 2024 theorem does not impose the involution, and its unrestricted optimizers have size 27, whereas our constrained optima have size 17, so the new statement is not a direct special case of its extremal classification. An unindexed priority collision remains a specific risk.

value.rationale: An exact natural finite constraint interaction for strand-independent frame markers: no prefix/suffix overlap and closure under Watson–Crick reverse complements are separately motivated. The 17 versus established 27 optimum measures a sharp 10-word capacity loss, while 32 full optimizers and four symmetry orbits give structural choice criteria. Four-letter four-base codes are the smallest natural DNA tetranucleotide setting; this is not a parameter renamed from an unrestricted theorem or an arbitrary subcollection. Claim is a finite coding invariant, not a promise of performance, coding capacity at other lengths, or application efficacy.
